explanation: In Swahili, safari means any journey, not only a trip to see wildlife. Swahili itself borrowed the word from the Arabic safar, travel.

claims.text: The English word 'safari' comes from Swahili safari.
The English word 'safari' does not come from Zulu, Afrikaans or Amharic.
In Swahili, safari means a journey or trip of any kind.
The Swahili word safari comes from Arabic safar, meaning travel or journey.

evidence.restatement: English took safari in the late 19th century from Kiswahili, the trade language of the East African coast, through travellers' accounts of caravan expeditions.

claimResults.note: Solved cold. Every major dictionary traces the English word to Swahili, first recorded in English in the 1850s to 1890s (Burton and later East African travel writing). High-risk etymology held at certain confidence; memo 18 needs B's direct confirmation as well. No search spent: the cap is 2 and this etymology is uncontested.

evidence.restatement: Neither the South African languages Zulu and Afrikaans nor Ethiopian Amharic is the source; the word passed from Arabic to Swahili and from Swahili to English.

claimResults.note: Afrikaans is a well-chosen trap (it gave English trek, a close cousin in meaning) and Zulu is the famous southern Bantu language, but neither is in the chain. Amharic is Semitic like Arabic, yet the borrowing into English did not pass through it. None is defensible as the answer.

evidence.restatement: Swahili speakers use safari for travel in general, from a bus ride to a business trip; 'safari njema' wishes someone a good trip.

claimResults.note: Everyday Swahili usage; the wildlife sense is the narrowed English meaning.

evidence.restatement: The Swahili noun is a loan from the Arabic root s-f-r, as in safar, a journey.

claimResults.note: Swahili has a large Arabic loan layer from Indian Ocean trade, and this is one of the standard examples; dictionaries give Arabic safar (journey) as the source. Certain; memo 18 applies to the high-risk label.

evidence.restatement: English took safari in the 19th century from Swahili, which itself had it from Arabic.

claimResults.note: Rival test: Arabic is the ultimate source, but it is not offered, so the immediate-source reading leaves one key. The stem asks which language it came into English from, and standard dictionaries give Swahili. High risk (etymology) so it relies on check A's external evidence.

evidence.restatement: Safari is not a Zulu, Afrikaans or Amharic word in origin; Afrikaans and Zulu use other words for a trip, and the English borrowing is from East African Swahili.

claimResults.note: Afrikaans is the likeliest lure because of South African game reserves, but the word reached English from East Africa.

evidence.restatement: In Swahili safari is a general word for a journey or trip, not only a wildlife expedition.
Swahili safari is a loanword from Arabic safar, whose meaning is travel or a journey.
